Dakota

Dakota peoples include distinct communities and governments across a wide region. This Minnesota-focused reading path centers community accounts, Dakota public testimony and education, historical displacement, and a dated treaty record. It distinguishes Minnesota governments and specific historical evidence from broader Dakota identities and histories elsewhere.

A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

Thirteen substantive inspected works now support a Minnesota-focused introduction, including separate accounts from three Minnesota Dakota governments, the 2025 Upper Sioux Community account carried in a state guide, a Lower Sioux Community-produced history booklet, Dakota-created education, named Dakota public testimony, a specific 1851 treaty text and focused state records. New community pages add distinct Prairie Island preservation and language-program material and Shakopee language education. Seven supporting references remain excluded. This is still weighted toward Minnesota and institutional materials, not a deep history of every Dakota community, specialist language study, current demographic account or community-reviewed collection.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • The Upper Sioux Community government website returned HTTP 403 to this research request. The accessible state-hosted histories and 2025 government guide provide useful community-attributed material, but the current Community constitution, official land-conveyance instrument, and a direct government publication about the 2024 return remain unreviewed; the access failure is not treated as a paywall and was not bypassed.
  • Dakota communities outside Minnesota, including particular governments in the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Canada, need their own community voices and scoped sources. This collection is not an exhaustive homeland or present-community map.
  • Specialist Dakota language scholarship is needed for precise language variation and classification; undated public speaker totals should not be used as current demographic findings.
  • Original treaty scans, oral understandings, 1863 statutes, community constitutions, and additional Dakota-authored historical scholarship would deepen the collection. Treaty text, state summaries, and public exhibition testimony answer different questions.
  • The complete Mni Sóta Maḳoce lesson materials require teacher training; the public page gives the curriculum overview but not the lessons themselves. Outcome research was described by the publisher as forthcoming, so no effectiveness claim is made.
  • Dated education reports and community evaluations would be needed before describing current operations, participation, or outcomes. No clinical, legal, membership, or service-eligibility conclusion is proposed.
  • No Dakota community review or endorsement is recorded.
  • The MNHS Dean Blue oral-history source is a short excerpt; its full interview was not verified through the archive link and the individual's view does not establish a Dakota-wide position.
01

Cansa'yapi: community continuity and public history

The Lower Sioux Indian Community identifies its members as Mdewakanton Dakota and calls its Minnesota River homeland Caŋṡayapi. Its account describes families returning despite exile. A companion historic-site page dates tribal management of the Lower Sioux Agency site to 2007. The Community’s public history booklet adds its own account of Caŋṡayapi, stewardship, sovereignty, the 1851–1858 treaty period, community continuity after 1862, Wacipi and Dakota-language renewal. These are community-specific historical and educational statements, not independent verification of broader Dakota history or a homeland boundary. Together the sources connect continuity with the Community’s authority to interpret a place shaped by federal reservation policy.

Read the sources [1] Lower Sioux Indian Community [21] Lower Sioux Indian Community; hosted by the Minnesota Department of Education

02

A particular Mdewakanton government's institutions

The SMSC identifies itself as a Dakota government within the Oceti Ṡakowiŋ, alongside related Dakota, Lakota and Nakota peoples. Its public timeline follows forced removal, later land purchases and its own 1969 governmental organization. The community dates Hoċokata Ṫi's opening to 2019. These are a particular Mdewakanton government's institutions, not a model shared by every Dakota community.

Read the sources [2] Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community

03

Prairie Island's account of land and persistence

Prairie Island identifies its members as Bdewakantunwan, or Mdewakanton, Eastern Dakota. Its history follows families who remained or returned, purchased land and maintained a community despite displacement. The Tribe also describes pressures from dam construction, a nuclear generating plant and rail transport. These concerns are its situated account of Prairie Island, rather than a general description of every Dakota homeland.

Read the sources [3] Prairie Island Indian Community

04

Language activism across community boundaries

Dakota Wicohan traces its origins to a 2001 language team involving Upper Sioux, Lower Sioux and Twin Cities Dakota, followed by nonprofit incorporation in 2002. Its account connects intergenerational language learning, teacher preparation and outreach with community relationships. This educational organization works across political boundaries; it is not another tribal government. Its undated speaker and program totals are not current measurements. A separate Dakota Wicohan curriculum was developed by Dakota scholars and educators led by Iyekiyapiwiƞ Darlene St. Clair. Its ten-lesson outline treats Minnesota as Dakota homeland and covers place, language, sovereignty, treaties, colonization, cultural continuity and living together. The public overview says teachers need training to access the lessons and that outcome research was still forthcoming; the materials have not been presented here as an evaluated program.

Read the sources [4] Dakota Wicohan [12] Dakota Wicohan

05

Imprisonment and forced removal

MNHS describes noncombatant Dakota imprisonment at Fort Snelling during 1862–1863 and forced transport to Crow Creek in May 1863. It distinguishes congressional actions of February 16 and March 3, 1863, concerning treaty annulment and removal. Its account also discusses a separate Ho-Chunk expulsion. These histories should not be conflated or taken to mean every Dakota person participated in the war.

Read the sources [5] Minnesota Historical Society

06

Reading the 1851 Mendota treaty carefully

The Mendota treaty text names Mdewakanton and Wahpekute parties, rather than every Dakota community. Its published version records a land cession, differentiated payments and funding for education and farms. It also marks Article 3 as deleted and prints supplemental terms. This specific written federal record does not establish fully informed consent, oral understandings, promise fulfillment or present individual entitlements.

Read the sources [6] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; transcription of 10 Stat. 954

07

Four Minnesota governments within wider Dakota peoples

MnDOT's public inventory names Lower Sioux, Prairie Island, Shakopee Mdewakanton and Upper Sioux as Minnesota Dakota communities. Each government needs its own institutional reading. This four-government inventory is a Minnesota access point, not an exhaustive list of Dakota peoples or their communities elsewhere in the United States and Canada.

Read the sources [7] Minnesota Department of Transportation

08

Earlier reading links and their limits

The retained South Dakota teaching-kit versions offer a broad comparative educational starting point; only their contents and goals were inspected here. The retained Black Hills page identifies a hosted student legal position paper. These resources do not supply Minnesota Dakota community authority, a universal cultural description or verified current law, and remain outside this collection's substantive count.

Read the sources [8] South Dakota State Historical Society [9] South Dakota State Historical Society [10] Lakota Dakota Nakota Nation website, using its own institutional self-description

09

Homeland through named Dakota voices

In the Minnesota Historical Society’s Our Home exhibition transcript, five named Dakota speakers describe Minnesota as Dakota homeland, discuss the Seven Council Fires, and speak about relationships to land and relatives. The speakers use different formulations: Dallas Ross distinguishes Dakota as a way of life from a nation of people, while Grace Goldtooth-Campos refers to Dakota Oyate as a nation and describes its council-fire groups. Keeping each statement attributed makes the variation visible without treating one exhibition transcript as a universal definition for all Dakota people or governments. In a separate MNHS oral-history excerpt, Upper Sioux narrator Dean Blue reflects on Fort Snelling from his own experience as a veteran-service officer and expresses a personal view about the building. The interviewer notes that Dakota people held differing views; the excerpt should be read as one individual's public memory, not as consensus.

Read the sources [13] Minnesota Historical Society [20] Minnesota Historical Society

10

Upper Sioux Community: Pezihutazizi Oyate and returned agency lands

The 2025 Minnesota Tribal Government guide presents Upper Sioux Community’s account of Pejuhutazizi Kapi as Dakota homeland, the community’s formation in 1938 on 746 returned acres, and its 1995 constitution. The guide reports that the state returned the former Upper Sioux Agency State Park in 2024 and gives a resulting total land base of 3,725 acres; its membership count is a dated 2025 report figure, not a current 2026 measure. The Minnesota DNR describes the Community’s long-standing request and explains the 1862 history of starvation and death at the agency, while Minnesota law records the state’s direction to transfer park land. The DNR page and statute are state records, not substitutes for the Community’s own historical account. A separate undated state-hosted version repeats the community history with older acreage and population figures; neither version defines all Dakota homelands or a present boundary.

Read the sources [11] Minnesota Secretary of State; the profile presents the Upper Sioux Community’s account [14] Minnesota Department of Natural Resources [15] Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes [16] Minnesota Indian Affairs Council; page uses first-person community language and links to the Upper Sioux Community

11

Language renewal within Prairie Island and Shakopee communities

Prairie Island describes its community language department, classes, culture camps, language-bowl activities and outreach at Red Wing High School. Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community describes its own language team, weekly classes, family learning events, youth camps and Dakota-language education. These are two governments’ accounts of particular programs, not a single uniform Dakota-language system. Prairie Island’s page still refers to an app expected in spring 2023; its present availability was not verified.

Read the sources [17] Prairie Island Indian Community [18] Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community

12

Prairie Island’s cultural and historic preservation work

Prairie Island describes its Tribal Historic Preservation Office, artifact repatriation work, restoration of the public He Mni Can site, and partnership to protect the Grand Meadow Chert Quarry. These examples show the Community’s own preservation priorities and public interpretation. Its broader archaeological statements remain attributed to the Community; no burial locations or restricted details are repeated.

Read the sources [19] Prairie Island Indian Community

What needs further research

  • The Upper Sioux Community government website returned HTTP 403 to this research request. The accessible state-hosted histories and 2025 government guide provide useful community-attributed material, but the current Community constitution, official land-conveyance instrument, and a direct government publication about the 2024 return remain unreviewed; the access failure is not treated as a paywall and was not bypassed.
  • Dakota communities outside Minnesota, including particular governments in the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Canada, need their own community voices and scoped sources. This collection is not an exhaustive homeland or present-community map.
  • Specialist Dakota language scholarship is needed for precise language variation and classification; undated public speaker totals should not be used as current demographic findings.
  • Original treaty scans, oral understandings, 1863 statutes, community constitutions, and additional Dakota-authored historical scholarship would deepen the collection. Treaty text, state summaries, and public exhibition testimony answer different questions.
  • The complete Mni Sóta Maḳoce lesson materials require teacher training; the public page gives the curriculum overview but not the lessons themselves. Outcome research was described by the publisher as forthcoming, so no effectiveness claim is made.
  • Dated education reports and community evaluations would be needed before describing current operations, participation, or outcomes. No clinical, legal, membership, or service-eligibility conclusion is proposed.
  • No Dakota community review or endorsement is recorded.

Substantive works and supporting access routes are counted separately. Actual selected inspection scope and dates appear on the cards; unread references and source media are not counted. This is a Minnesota-focused initial source guide, not a complete history of Dakota peoples or a community endorsement. Governance, historical, educational, and language claims retain their particular community, speaker, source, and period. Three additional community-government pages reviewed on 2026-10-23 describe Prairie Island language education and cultural preservation and Shakopee Dakota-language programs. Their program descriptions are community-specific; an older anticipated app launch is not treated as current status, and linked lessons or dictionaries were not counted as inspected. The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council’s undated Upper Sioux page reports 453 people and more than 900 acres, while the 2025 Minnesota Tribal Government guide reports a 2024 return and a 3,725-acre total land base and prints a 577 membership figure. The records are dated differently; no number is treated as a current 2026 figure, and none defines a homeland boundary. No historical map association was added. The Minnesota regional route is a navigation aid and does not describe the extent of Dakota homelands. 2026-10-23 follow-up: read the full visible MNHS story page for a short Dean Blue oral-history excerpt on Fort Snelling and the interview metadata. The full interview link returned HTTP 404 during inspection; a search-discovered copy with unverified hosting provenance was not relied on. Added as supporting testimony only (countsTowardMinimum:false); the interviewer's prompt records differing Dakota views. 2026-10-23 follow-up: read selected substantive sections of the Lower Sioux Indian Community’s 19-page Caŋṡayapi history booklet hosted by Minnesota Department of Education. Added as a community-produced work for its scoped Lower Sioux history, homeland/treaty account, governance, site stewardship and language-education coverage. General historical claims are attributed; maps in the booklet were not separately catalogued. Dakota now has thirteen substantive inspected works; initial adequacy remains Still unfinished.

Minnesota Laws 2023, Chapter 60, section 97 — Upper Sioux Agency State Park land transfer ↗

Publication: 2023

Section 97 directs the commissioner of natural resources to convey state-owned land within Upper Sioux Agency State Park to the Upper Sioux Community without consideration; it separately authorizes a possible Minnesota Historical Society conveyance subject to Executive Council approval and legal barriers. The statute records the state’s authorization and requirements, not an independent account of Dakota history or proof of every step of conveyance.

Dean Blue on Fort Snelling — U.S.-Dakota War oral-history excerpt ↗

Publication: Interview recorded April 27, 2011; web page dated July 24, 2026

This MNHS page publishes a short excerpt from an interview recorded in Granite Falls in 2011. Blue reflects on visits to Fort Snelling through his veteran-service work and gives his own view of whether the fort should remain. The interviewer's framing explicitly notes differing Dakota views, so this is one person's perspective, not community consensus or a general Dakota position. It is evidence about a named narrator's public memory, not independent verification of historical events.

Inspection: Supporting or limited review; see scope

Scope: Read the complete visible story page, including the transcript excerpt (lines 80–100), its citation and interview metadata. The MNHS-linked full oral-history record returned HTTP 404 during inspection; this does not establish a reader access restriction. A search-discovered copy with unverified hosting provenance was not relied on. This excerpt is retained as supporting testimony and does not count toward the substantive-work target.

Ehaŋna k’a Dehan: Past and Present — Caŋṡayapi community history booklet ↗

Publication: Undated; no publication date displayed in the inspected PDF

This 19-page community-produced booklet introduces Caŋṡayapi (Lower Sioux) through community history, relationships to the Minnesota River Valley, stewardship, sovereignty, the Lower Sioux Agency site, Wacipi and Dakota language. It says the Community traces its lineage primarily to Mdewakanton Dakota, and describes Wahpekute relationships and wider Oceti Ṡakowiŋ connections. Community historical and homeland statements are attributed to this publication; they are not independently verified by this review or a boundary determination. Historic acreage and membership figures elsewhere in the booklet are not treated as current measurements.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Read selected substantive sections in the publicly accessible 19-page PDF: community introduction and relationship to the land (PDF pp. 2–4); land, stewardship and homeland/treaty history (pp. 6–12); Wacipi and language (pp. 14–16); and the historic-site and resource/back-cover context (pp. 17–19). Reviewed the visible resource list and map captions, but did not extract the map as a separate historical-map record. Other material and linked resources were not claimed as read.
